core_insight: Hexagonal architecture isolates business logic from frameworks by making the domain depend only on ports it owns, so delivery mechanisms can change without touching core rules.

scenes.voice: Why does a working order service suddenly become hard to change? Because the domain started calling HttpServletRequest, JPA, Kafka, and Stripe directly.
scenes.visual: Code snippet showing OrderService with direct imports to Spring, JPA, Kafka, Stripe, then red coupling arrows pointing outward.

scenes.voice: The real problem isn't code, it's change. You want to test rules without a database, expose the same logic via REST, gRPC, CLI, and swap Stripe for Adyen without touching business rules.
scenes.visual: List of change needs appearing with check marks: test without DB, multiple interfaces, swap payment.

scenes.voice: Layered architecture helps, but the domain still knows about delivery. The coupling direction is wrong: business logic depends on frameworks, not the other way around.
scenes.visual: Simple layered diagram with arrows from Domain down to Frameworks, highlighted as bad direction.

scenes.voice: Hexagonal flips it. Core is the hexagon. Ports are contracts the core owns. Adapters plug in from outside. Core knows only ports, never adapters. Adapters depend on core.
scenes.visual: Hexagon with Core in center, Ports on edges, Adapters outside. Arrows point inward.
scenes.mermaid:
graph LR
    UI[Web / CLI / gRPC] --> InAdapter[Inbound Adapter]
    InAdapter --> InPort[Inbound Port]
    InPort --> Core[Domain Core]
    Core --> OutPort[Outbound Port]
    OutPort --> OutAdapter[Outbound Adapter]
    OutAdapter --> DB[(Database)]
    OutAdapter --> MQ[Message Bus]
    OutAdapter --> Payment[Payment API]

scenes.voice: Inbound ports are use cases like CreateOrder. Outbound ports are capabilities the core needs like PersistOrder, ChargeCard. Adapters translate HTTP to DTOs, DB to entities, SDK to domain.
scenes.visual: Zoom into ports: Inbound Port labeled OrderApplicationService, Outbound Port labeled OrderRepository, PaymentGateway. Adapter boxes show REST controller, JPA repo, Stripe adapter.

scenes.voice: What do you gain? You can test domain rules with in-memory fakes, reuse the same core in API and worker, and replace Postgres or Stripe by writing a new adapter. What do you pay? Indirection and boilerplate. For CRUD apps with little domain behavior, that's overhead.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left gains with green check, right costs with yellow warning. Show fake PaymentGateway in test.

scenes.voice: Use it when business logic is long-lived and delivery is volatile. Don't use it when it just creates UserRepositoryPort, Adapter, Impl for no reason. Keep core rich with behavior, adapters thin with translation.
scenes.visual: Decision flow: Domain stable + multiple interfaces? Yes → Hexagonal. Just CRUD? No → keep simple. Core with behavior highlighted.

mental_model: Think of the app as a hexagon: core business logic in the middle, ports are the only contracts it knows, adapters are replaceable plugs on the outside. Dependency always points inward.
final_takeaway: Isolate business logic from frameworks via ports and adapters so changing transport, persistence, or third-party SDKs is an adapter change, not a core change.
